passage:
Diary, Monday.
Our class has a book shelf with no lock. Rule: take one, leave one, write your name in the register. Today I saw Minakshi take two comics and leave none. I almost said nothing, since she's my friend. But if everyone did that, the shelf would be empty in a week, and Ma'am trusted us enough not to lock it. So at break I told her quietly. "Sorry, Nilesh," she said. "I forgot to bring one." Tomorrow she'll bring two. I'm glad I said it. It's not about Ma'am catching us. It's about all of us keeping it working.

qa.q: What is the rule for the class book shelf?
qa.a: Take one, leave one, and write your name in the register.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh almost say nothing?
qa.a: Nilesh didn't want to trouble a friend, but also felt the shelf only works if everyone keeps the rule.

qa.q: What did Nilesh's quiet approach get right?
qa.a: Nilesh spoke privately, which let Minakshi fix it without being shamed, and kept the trust-based rule alive.

qa.q: How might Ma'am feel if she heard about this?
qa.a: Pleased that the class is keeping the system fair on its own, showing her trust was well placed.

grounding: It shows a child upholding a shared rule because the system depends on everyone's trust, not on being caught.

passage: At the village hand pump, the rule was simple: one bucket each, then back of the line. Nobody enforced it; it worked because everyone did it. Jasleen, eleven, was fourth in line when her cousin Amandeep ran up. "Let me go before you, just this once. Mummy's shouting." Jasleen looked at the three women behind her, their buckets waiting. "If I let you, they'll let their cousins, and nobody gets water on time." Then she added, "Stand behind me, and I'll help you carry yours after." Amandeep sighed, but got in line.

qa.q: What is the rule at the hand pump?
qa.a: One bucket each, then back of the line.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen look at the women behind her before answering?
qa.a: She was concerned about fairness to them, knowing the line only works if everyone keeps to it.

qa.q: What made Jasleen's answer both fair and kind?
qa.a: She kept the rule but offered to help carry Amandeep's bucket, so Amandeep wasn't simply turned away.

qa.q: What would change if Jasleen had let Amandeep skip?
qa.a: Others might start letting their relatives in too, and the trust that keeps the line working could break down.

grounding: It shows a girl keeping a shared queue rule because it rests on everyone's mutual trust.

passage: In their school in Accra, the rule on the veranda was that bags stayed open on the bench during football, and nobody touched anyone else's. After the game Kofi, twelve, found a folded cedi note on the floor beside Nadia's bag. Some boys said, "Finders keepers." Kofi shook his head. "Last month she found my watch and gave it back. If we start taking stuff, we'll all have to carry our bags onto the pitch." He handed Nadia the note. She said, "I owe you a mango." He laughed. "You owe me nothing. That's the deal."

qa.q: What did Kofi find beside Nadia's bag?
qa.a: A folded cedi note.

qa.q: Why did Kofi think of the watch Nadia had returned?
qa.a: He felt that trust works both ways, and since she had been honest with him, he wanted to be honest with her.

qa.q: How could Kofi respond if the boys keep saying "finders keepers"?
qa.a: Explain simply that the bench only stays safe if everyone returns things, as he just did.

qa.q: How does Nadia see Kofi returning the money?
qa.a: She is grateful and wants to repay him, showing the give-and-take that keeps their trust going.

grounding: It shows a boy keeping an unwritten rule out of reciprocity and the trust it protects.

passage: At the school canteen, Manjula Aunty gave Ritu change for her samosa. Walking back, Ritu counted: ten rupees too much. Her friend said, 'Keep it, she won't notice.' Ritu stopped. 'She trusts us. If we all kept extra, she'd lose money, and then she'd stop letting us pay later when we forget cash.' She went back. 'Aunty, you gave me extra.' Manjula smiled. 'Thank you, Ritu. You can pay tomorrow anytime you're short.'

qa.q: How much extra change did Ritu get?
qa.a: She got ten rupees too much.

qa.q: Why did Ritu decide to return the money?
qa.a: She thought about fairness and trust, realising that keeping it would hurt Aunty and break the trust between them.

qa.q: What does Ritu's choice show about following rules?
qa.a: It shows following fair rules can keep trust going both ways, which benefits everyone.

qa.q: How might Manjula Aunty see Ritu after this?
qa.a: She will likely trust Ritu more and be even more willing to help her. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child internalising fairness and rule-following based on mutual trust at a school canteen.

passage: I watch Suraj and Ojas play cricket in the lane from my window every evening. Yesterday Ojas hit the ball into Mrs. Mehta's garden. They'd agreed that was out. Ojas said, 'But it was a great shot!' Suraj shook his head. 'We said garden is out. If we change it now, why have rules?' Ojas frowned but handed over the bat. Later, Suraj was out the same way, and he gave the bat back without arguing. They're younger than me, but they're fairer than most grown-ups.

qa.q: Where did Ojas hit the ball?
qa.a: Ojas hit it into Mrs. Mehta's garden.

qa.q: What does Ojas frowning but handing over the bat suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Ojas felt disappointed but accepted the rule because they had both agreed to it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Suraj following the same rule when he got out showed fairness, which kept their trust and the game going.

qa.q: How does the narrator see Suraj and Ojas?
qa.a: The narrator admires them, seeing them as fairer than most grown-ups.

grounding: Shows children following agreed rules out of mutual fairness and trust, observed by a neighbour.

passage: Week one: Bidisha and Parul, both ten, agreed to share Bidisha's cycle: half an hour each, turn by turn. Bidisha always brought it back on time. Week two: Parul kept it for an hour and said, "You didn't need it." Bidisha felt cheated but still returned it on time the next day. "If I break the rule, it stops working," she told her mother. Week three: Parul apologised. "You kept your side, so I'll keep mine." They wrote the rule on a card and stuck it on the cycle.

qa.q: How long was each turn with the cycle?
qa.a: Half an hour each.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel when Parul kept the cycle for an hour?
qa.a: She felt cheated and hurt, but still wanted to keep her side of the deal.

qa.q: Which choice kept the deal alive, and why?
qa.a: Bidisha still returning on time, because it built trust and made Parul want to be fair too.

qa.q: How might Parul see the deal after week two?
qa.a: She realises Bidisha trusted her and feels she should keep her side.

grounding: Shows a child keeping a fair rule based on trust and reciprocity, even when her friend breaks it.

passage: "Hrithik, you asked why I always pay exactly. When I, your Farida Dadi, was eleven, the mango seller in our village left his basket and a tin by the road while he worked in the field. We children could take one mango and drop a coin in. One day my friend took two and paid for one. I said, 'If we cheat, he'll stop trusting us, and then no one gets mangoes.' She laughed at me, but she put the second coin in. That old man trusted us for years."

qa.q: Where did the mango seller leave his basket and tin?
qa.a: By the road.

qa.q: What might young Farida have felt when her friend took two mangoes?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and upset, worried that the cheating would break the seller's trust.

qa.q: What turning point in the story kept the system working?
qa.a: Farida speaking up and her friend paying the second coin.

qa.q: How might the mango seller have felt about the village children?
qa.a: He probably felt trusting and grateful, since they kept the honesty system for years.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a childhood rule based on mutual trust and why keeping it mattered.

passage: On a hot afternoon the class teacher was called away, and the substitute didn't come. Class 7 was alone for forty minutes. There was one water cooler and thirty thirsty children. Arohi, twelve, stood near it. "One glass each, then back of the line," she said. Kavitha frowned. "Who made you boss?" "Nobody. It's just fair. We all need water." A few boys pushed, but most joined the line. When the teacher came back, the class was noisy but calm, and everyone had had water.

qa.q: How long was the class alone?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What might Arohi have felt when Kavitha asked "Who made you boss?"
qa.a: She may have felt a little stung but stayed calm, sure that fairness mattered more.

qa.q: What made Arohi's rule work?
qa.a: It was simple, fair to everyone, and most children trusted it would give them a turn.

qa.q: How might Kavitha see Arohi's rule once she has had her water?
qa.a: She might accept it as fair, even if she didn't like being told at first.

grounding: Shows a child upholding a fair rule based on trust when no adult is present.

passage: Zubin lent Pradeep his cycle on Saturday morning in the Chandigarh colony. "Back by six," Zubin said. "I need it for tuition." At half past five, Pradeep was still racing round the park with the others. "One more round!" someone shouted. Pradeep looked at the sky. "No, I promised Zubin." He rode back and handed it over at ten to six. Zubin smiled. "You're on time." "You trusted me," Pradeep said. "Next time I'll lend you my skates." Zubin grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: By what time did Zubin want the cycle back?
qa.a: By six.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he decided to go back?
qa.a: He felt torn: tempted to keep playing, but uneasy about breaking his promise to Zubin.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Returning the cycle on time, because it kept Zubin's trust and led to more sharing.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Pradeep after this?
qa.a: Zubin likely trusts him more and is happy to share again.

grounding: A boy returns a borrowed cycle on time because he values trust and reciprocity.

passage:
"It's my turn to choose the show," said Rashmi.
"No, you chose yesterday," Darshan said.
"But you got the last samosa."
"That's not the same thing!"
Rashmi crossed her arms. "Fine. What's fair?"
Darshan thought. "We made a rule: Monday me, Tuesday you, and so on."
"Today's Wednesday."
"So it's me."
Rashmi scowled, then sighed. "Okay. But tomorrow I choose, no matter what."
"Deal. And you can have the next samosa."
Rashmi laughed. "Now that's fair."

qa.q: What day was it?
qa.a: Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she scowled and then sighed?
qa.a: She felt annoyed at first, then accepting, because the rule they made was fair.

qa.q: What helped them settle the argument?
qa.a: Remembering the rule they had agreed on and offering something back.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Rashmi's final agreement?
qa.a: He likely feels relieved and respected that she kept to the rule.

grounding: A brother and sister settle a TV argument by relying on their agreed turn-taking rule.

passage: I'm Jahnavi. Our Class 6 has an honour shelf of storybooks. There's no teacher watching; you write your name in the register and bring the book back in a week. Last month I took a mystery and forgot it at Nani's. Harsha asked, "Where's the book? I'm next." My stomach dropped. I made Papa drive to Nani's that evening to get it, and returned it the next day. I realised the shelf only works if everyone brings books back. If people stop, then no one trusts anyone. Now I set a reminder on the fridge.

qa.q: How long do students have to return a book?
qa.a: A week.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel when Harsha asked where the book was?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt guilty and worried, with a stomach that dropped.

qa.q: What could help Jahnavi return books on time in future?
qa.a: Jahnavi now sets a reminder on the fridge, which is a simple way to remember.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Jahnavi's effort to get the book back?
qa.a: Harsha likely feels respected and trusts Jahnavi to keep to the shelf rules.

grounding: A child reflects on why the class honour shelf depends on everyone returning books.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Tuesday.

Our class library runs on trust: children borrow books and return them by Friday, and nobody checks.

Yusuf finished his book early but kept it to read again. On Friday, he brought it back even though he wanted it longer. When I asked, he said, "If I keep it, someone else can't read it. And then nobody will trust the library."

I told him he could borrow it again next week. — Kiran

qa.q: When do the children return library books?
qa.a: They return them by Friday.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel about returning the book?
qa.a: Yusuf felt a bit reluctant, wanting to read it again, but responsible to the class.

qa.q: How did Kiran encourage Yusuf's fairness?
qa.a: Kiran said he could borrow it again next week.

qa.q: How might other children feel about the library if everyone did what Yusuf did?
qa.a: They would feel trusted and fairly treated, knowing books come back on time.

grounding: A teacher notes a boy returning a library book on time because the system depends on mutual trust.

passage:
Summer holidays, Thursday

Played the board game with Uday all afternoon. When I went to get water, he said, "Let's move my token three extra places, nobody will know."

I said no. He said I was boring.

But if we cheat, the game doesn't mean anything. And next time he'd cheat against me.

So we played properly. I lost. It was still fun.

At the end Uday said, "Okay, you're right. It's better when it's fair."

Sunaina

qa.q: How many extra places did Uday want to move his token?
qa.a: Uday wanted to move his token three extra places.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Uday called Sunaina boring?
qa.a: Sunaina felt a bit hurt but firm, believing cheating would spoil the game.

qa.q: What did Sunaina understand about rules?
qa.a: That rules only work when everyone trusts each other, and cheating would make the game meaningless.

qa.q: How did Uday's view change?
qa.a: Uday first wanted to cheat but later agreed it was better when it's fair.

grounding: A child refuses to cheat in a game because rules work only when players trust each other.

passage:
During the wheat harvest, the handpump in the village near Bareilly had a long line of children with buckets. Sunaina, ten, was fifth.

Farhan came late. "My Abbu needs water fast for the thresher. Let me go first."

Sunaina looked at the line. "Everyone's parents are in the fields."

"But I'm older."

"Then you know the rule. We go in turn."

The others nodded. Farhan huffed but joined the back.

When Sunaina's turn came, she filled her bucket quickly, then helped Farhan carry his to the front of the line when it was his turn.

qa.q: What position was Sunaina in line?
qa.a: Sunaina was fifth.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Farhan asked to go first?
qa.a: Sunaina felt calm but determined, and a little annoyed, believing the rule should apply to everyone.

qa.q: What did Sunaina do that showed fairness and kindness?
qa.a: She kept the turn rule, then helped Farhan carry his bucket when it was his turn.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel after joining the back?
qa.a: Farhan might feel annoyed at first but later grateful for Sunaina's help.

grounding: During the harvest, a girl upholds a fair turn-taking rule at a village handpump based on mutual trust.

passage: On Halloween night in Houston, Tuan and Diego made a deal before they set out: whatever they collected would go into one bag and be split evenly at the end. At the last house, a neighbour gave Tuan a big chocolate bar while Diego was tying his shoe. Tuan slipped it into his jacket. Walking home, the bar felt heavy. On the porch Diego counted out the sweets, one for you, one for me, careful as always. "Wait," Tuan said, and pulled out the bar. "This goes in too. We said everything." Diego broke it in half. "Next year you're my partner again."

qa.q: What did the neighbour give Tuan at the last house?
qa.a: A big chocolate bar.

qa.q: Why did the bar feel heavy to Tuan on the walk home?
qa.a: He felt guilty about breaking the deal with Diego and uneasy keeping it secret.

qa.q: Which choice kept the friendship strong, and why?
qa.a: Adding the bar to the pile kept the deal they both trusted, so Diego wants to partner again.

qa.q: How does Diego see Tuan when the bar comes out?
qa.a: Diego sees Tuan as fair and trustworthy, and rewards the honesty by asking Tuan to be a partner again next year.

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping a fair-sharing deal with a friend because they trust each other.
